extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of literature, dramatists and creative writers studying tragedy
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for creating or analyzing hamartia (the tragic error/flaw) in dramatic literature — what counts as a tragic mistake, how it functions in plot, and how it should affect audience response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protagonist's error as causal driver (hamartia definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: The protagonist's error that leads to a chain of actions which culminate in a reversal of events from felicity to disaster.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamartia is commonly understood as the mistake or error at the center of the tragic plot; it must link actions into a causal chain producing peripeteia (reversal) and catastrophe. The entry emphasizes the error's causal role rather than merely a descriptive label.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitted kinds of error (types of hamartia)
rubrics_metrics.description: What qualifies as the error or flaw varies and can include an error resulting from ignorance, an error of judgment, an inherent flaw in the character, or a wrongdoing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors/analysts should consider a spectrum: intellectual errors (lack of information), errors of judgment, innate character defects, or moral wrongs. The page notes debate over which of these are primary; any of them may serve as hamartia if they produce the tragic chain of events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral neutrality of hamartia
rubrics_metrics.description: Hamartia is a morally neutral, non‑normative term derived from 'to miss the mark', not necessarily implying fault, vice, guilt, or moral deficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid conflating hamartia with moral condemnation. The concept can denote inadvertent mistake or misapprehension rather than vice; treating it neutrally helps explain tragedies where the hero acts in good faith but with disastrous results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evoking pity and fear leading to catharsis
rubrics_metrics.description: Hamartia should drive actions that inspire in the audience a build of pity and fear that leads to a purgation of those emotions (catharsis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The tragic error should be constructed so the audience identifies with the protagonist's plight (pity) and feels fear at the reversal; this emotional architecture is central to Aristotle's purpose for tragedy. Use inner motivations that make the fall intelligible and affecting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protagonist status and adequate magnitude
rubrics_metrics.description: For a story to be 'of adequate magnitude' it involves characters of high rank, prestige, or good fortune; the protagonist should be neither exceptionally virtuous nor too wicked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a protagonist whose change of fortune is significant enough to produce pity/fear. If too admirable or too villainous, the required emotional balance for catharsis will not be achieved. This is a guideline for scale and moral complexity of tragic heroes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding simplistic 'tragic flaw' explanations (critical caution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics and students often reduce hamartia to a single named 'flaw' (e.g., 'thinking too much' for Hamlet), which can be misleading and fail to explain contradictory actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing or writing, ensure the identified error accounts for the protagonist's range of behaviors; prefer interpretations (like ignorance of key facts) that coherently explain multiple decisions rather than a superficial personality label.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protagonist as agent of own suffering (tragic irony requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: A defining feature of tragedy is that the sufferer must be the agent of his own suffering without conscious moral failing in order to create tragic irony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct hamartia so the protagonist's choices (even if made in good faith or ignorance) are the immediate cause of downfall; this preserves tragic irony and prevents external deus ex machina explanations from undermining the tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of divine intervention or fate (interaction with hamartia)
rubrics_metrics.description: Debates exist over whether gods/fate play a role; hamartia may include elements of fate or divine will, but plot action must still beget plot action in Aristotelian terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If incorporating fate/divine forces, ensure they interact with human error in a way that preserves causal chains. Critics differ (some see divine guidance in examples like Oedipus), so be explicit how supernatural elements relate to the protagonist's error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hamartia located at juncture between character and action
rubrics_metrics.description: The source of hamartia is at the juncture between character and the character's actions or behaviors; character reveals moral purpose — what agents seek or avoid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating/assessing hamartia, analyze how inner qualities (desires, fears, aims) translate into choices. The error should arise from that intersection so that it feels motivated by character while still producing catastrophic consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholarly/interpretive plurality (use as analytic concept)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scholars differ on definitions—hamartia has been read as 'single great error', 'defect in character', intellectual mistake, or a matter including but distinct from divine retribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers and critics should be aware of multiple interpretive frameworks. Use the reading that best fits the work: moral-flaw readings suit some neoclassical tragedies; error/ignorance readings better explain works like Oedipus. Be explicit about which sense you employ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Christian-theological usages of hamartia
rubrics_metrics.description: In Christian theology hamartia (from Septuagint/New Testament usage) has four basic usages: acts of sin, original sin/fall, weakness of the flesh (propensity to sin), and personified sin (enslavement to sin).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When borrowing or invoking 'hamartia' outside classical drama, note the theological senses. For writers working with religious themes, choose the theological meaning intentionally (e.g., hamartia as personal failing versus systemic/original condition).
